newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: AMF sees $4.5 bln zinc reserves at Kipushi.
newsitem.headline: AMF sees $4.5 bln zinc reserves at Kipushi.

text.p: America Mineral Fields Inc believes the Kipushi zinc mine on the Zambian and former Zairean border has proven and probable in situ reserves worth $4.5 billion.
Kipushi halted production in 1993 due to lack of funds under the regime of former president Mobutu Sese Seko and is due to be restarted by AMF.
Production peaked in 1988 at 143,000 tonnes of zinc and 43,000 tonnes of copper.

AMF won the rights to rehabilitate the mine, process the zinc and copper tailings (waste) dam and build a 200,000 tonnes-a-year zinc smelter in April, after Laurent Kabila's alliance seized control of mineral-rich Shaba province, now Katanga.
AMF will revamp and develop the mine as part of a joint venture with the state mining company Gecamines.
The company said it and Gecamines had yet to finalise percentage shareholdings and which operations would be run as joint ventures.

"Kipushi mine really ranks as one of the world's major zinc mines. It has in situ reserves, proven and probable, worth around $4.5 billion," AMF director Richard Garnett told a visiting delegation from Europe and the U.S.
"There is a framework agreement in place (to mine Kipushi) and we have to finish a feasibility study by April 1998."
Furthermore, the Kipushi ore body extends into Zambia, offering potential for exploration and possible exploitation.

"If we did put in a smelter then we'd need a long-term supply of ore. There is the potential to increase zinc production and we can find more ore on the Zambian side. If we could find more ore there, we could bring in the concentrate from Zambia," Garnett said.
But he added that potential border problems would have to be overcome before that part of the ore body could be developed.
Garnett said drilling at the existing Kipushi mine showed zinc grades near the bottom of the ore body -- reserves go down to 1,800 metres -- of between 20 and 25 percent.
"There is a massive increase in width of the ore body with depth, and grade increases too," he said.

Once fully rehabilitated, Kipushi could process 200,000 tonnes of zinc per year, 30,000 tonnes of copper and 400,000 tonnes of sulphuric acid. AMF believes the mine would lie within the lower quartile as far as operating costs are concerned.
Rehabilitation would entail three projects.

"To bring the mine back into production is fairly simple," Garnett said, adding that the mine had been maintained in working condition and restarting operations would mostly entail bringing in the necessary machinery.
He said AMF planned to complete the sinking of the No.1 internal shaft to 1,500 metres. It is unfinished by 20 metres.
Rehabilitating the underground mine would cost AMF about $13 million.
The second project would be processing 70 years or 25 million tonnes worth of tailings grading 2.25 percent zinc.
AMF said the potential value of the tailings was $800 million but Garnett added: "The project by itself is very marginal. It's not a project that excites us at all."
The third project is to build a zinc smelter.
"We are looking very closely at smelting the concentrate on site," Garnett said.
